newsitem.title: USA: U.S. soybean stockpile to be smallest since 1977.
newsitem.headline: U.S. soybean stockpile to be smallest since 1977.

text.p: The U.S. stockpile of soybeans will shrink by late summer to its smallest size in two decades because of heavy global demand for vegetable oil and protein meal, Agriculture Department forecast Wednesday.

In a monthly report on world crops and usage, USDA estimated only 140 million bushels of soybeans would be left in U.S. grain bins when this year's crop was ready for harvest. It was a cut of 15 million bushels from last month's forecast.
"Soybean ending stocks are lowered 15 million bushels, the lowest since (102.9 million bushels in) 1976/77 and the lowest relative to use since 1972/73," the department said.
Agriculture Department raised its estimate of season-average prices for soybeans by five to 15 cents to $6.75 to $7.25 a bushel, which would match or exceed the 1996 average.
"I think the bean number, you have to say, is bullish on the ending stocks figure," said Don Roose, president of U.S. Commodities.
The soybean stocks forecast was slightly lower than traders had expected.

Minor changes were made by the department in its forecasts for corn and wheat trade. Corn exports were again forecast at 1.9 billion bushels and ending stocks at 959 million bushels. Wheat exports, like a month ago, were estimated at 950 million bushels but ending stocks were raised to 474 million bushels, up five million bushels because of larger imports.
The forecast for soybean exports was boosted by five million bushels, to 905 million, and the soybean crush was raised by 10 million bushels.
U.S. cotton exports, following a large crop, were pegged at 6.50 million bales, up 200,000 bales due to strong foreign demand, and ending stocks at 4.45 million bales, down slightly.
